strengths: The paper asks a timely and scientifically useful question: whether VGGT’s feed-forward reconstruction behavior reflects internalized geometric structure or merely appearance priors. I assess it primarily as a Concept & Feasibility / mechanistic-analysis contribution rather than a new algorithm, so the lack of a new reconstruction method is not itself a weakness.

The study usefully triangulates layerwise probing, attention analysis, causal interventions, and controlled input perturbations. The temporal alignment between correspondence-sensitive heads in layers 10–16 and improved fundamental-matrix decoding around layers 12–14 is an interesting observation.

The synthetic ShapeNet/Blender setup provides exact cameras, correspondences, and scene attributes, enabling controlled changes in viewpoint, focal length, illumination, symmetry, and occlusion that would be difficult to isolate in real data.

The supplementary experiments improve the intervention evidence by progressively localizing ablations—from whole heads to cross-view attention for corresponding patches and finally individual correspondence entries. The comparison against early- and late-layer interventions is also useful.

The paper is generally clear, visually well organized, and candid about important limitations, including synthetic-data bias, textureless scenes disadvantaging SIFT, and the inability of its interventions to fully isolate correspondence computation from other functions of the same heads.
weaknesses: The central claim that VGGT has developed geometric understanding is not yet convincingly separated from its direct supervision. VGGT is trained to predict camera intrinsics and extrinsics, from which the fundamental matrix is deterministically computable. Decoding F from camera tokens—especially with a nonlinear two-layer MLP having a 512-dimensional hidden layer—is therefore expected and does not by itself demonstrate emergent reasoning. Essential controls are missing, including linear probes, parameter/count-matched probes, direct analytic F computed from VGGT’s camera-head outputs, random or untrained-feature baselines, and tests on genuinely unseen camera distributions.

The causal interpretation remains confounded. Heads are selected using correspondence accuracy and then ablated, but early/late heads are not matched for general importance, attention magnitude, or downstream influence. Removing entire heads can disrupt many computations besides matching. Even the most localized experiment uses ground-truth correspondence locations and shows almost no effect for four top heads in layer 14 (+0.2 px), with a large effect appearing only when heads across layers 12–15 are jointly altered (+10.2 px). Random-head, magnitude-matched, and correspondence-preserving control interventions are needed before concluding that correspondence matching causes the geometric representation.

The correspondence evidence is very small-scale: the principal analysis uses only five scenes, one focal length, and averages over camera configurations. There are no confidence intervals, seed variation, statistical tests, or per-scene results. The manuscript also does not adequately document visibility filtering, chance accuracy, the number of evaluated patch pairs, or sensitivity to the top-1 patch criterion.

The robustness evaluation is restricted to synthetic, mostly isolated ShapeNet objects and compares only against SIFT and SuperGlue pipelines. It omits stronger contemporary matchers and learned geometric systems discussed in the paper, such as LoFTR, LightGlue, DUSt3R/MASt3R, or VGGSfM. Because textureless synthetic renderings particularly disadvantage local-feature pipelines, the broad claim of superior robustness over classical methods is not supported beyond this controlled setting.

The manuscript does not clearly specify how VGGT’s fundamental matrix is obtained in the robustness and intervention experiments—whether from the trained probe, analytically from predicted camera parameters, or by another procedure. This ambiguity is consequential for interpreting comparisons with RANSAC-based estimators and for reproducibility.

The occlusion results do not establish inpainting or hallucination. Above-zero attention matching at a masked source patch may arise from positional information, visible context, or attention artifacts, and the target-view content remains visible. The paper does not measure reconstructed depth or 3D error specifically within occluded regions, compare against positional/chance controls, or test multiple mask appearances. Thus the claimed undesirable reconstruction hallucination is speculative.

The datasets and protocols contain reporting inconsistencies: the main text states 10 distinctive and 5 symmetric categories, whereas the supplement states 13 categories, lists only 12 names, and identifies four symmetric categories. Several results are reported as median error only on successful cases alongside an arbitrary 10-pixel failure threshold, which complicates fair comparison. No code/data release statement, probe seeds, uncertainty estimates, or compute details are provided.

Overall, the work contains promising and potentially publishable observations, but the current evidence does not sufficiently rule out straightforward task-supervision and ablation-confound explanations. The limited synthetic scope and missing methodological details make the paper a slight reject rather than a borderline accept.

strengths: The paper asks an important and timely question: whether a feed-forward 3D model internally uses multi-view geometry or primarily exploits learned appearance priors. An interpretability study of VGGT could have meaningful impact even without introducing a new reconstruction algorithm.

The controlled ShapeNet/Blender setup provides exact camera parameters, visibility, correspondences, and fundamental matrices, enabling interventions that would be difficult to conduct reliably on real data.

The combination of layer-wise probing, attention inspection, targeted ablations, and input perturbations is broader than a purely correlational visualization study. The supplementary experiment that removes attention specifically at ground-truth correspondence locations is particularly useful.

The observation that correspondence-like attention becomes prominent in middle layers, shortly before fundamental-matrix decoding improves, is interesting and may motivate stronger mechanistic studies. The authors also acknowledge important limitations concerning synthetic data and imperfect localization of their interventions.
weaknesses: The central premise of the probing experiment is seriously confounded. VGGT is directly supervised to predict camera intrinsics and extrinsics, and the fundamental matrix is a deterministic function of these quantities. Recovering F from the same camera token used by the camera head is therefore not convincing evidence of geometric understanding "beyond" supervised tasks. The paper needs comparisons to F computed from VGGT's predicted cameras and controls such as random/untrained models, DINO features, input-only baselines, shuffled representations, and probes for equally complex nuisance targets.

The two-layer, 512-hidden-unit MLP is a high-capacity nonlinear probe trained for 50 epochs on the same synthetic camera and rendering distribution used for evaluation. It can itself learn the mapping from pose-related features to F, so the layer-wise results do not establish that VGGT represents or applies epipolar geometry. Linear probes, capacity sweeps, cross-distribution tests, and probe selectivity controls are missing.

The causal claims are overstated. Ablating high-matching heads can destroy information or computation unrelated to correspondence. Early- and late-layer heads are not adequate controls because layer sensitivity differs. The paper lacks same-layer non-matching-head controls, random-location interventions matched in number and magnitude, and tests of downstream VGGT outputs such as pose, depth, or point maps. Even the authors concede that the interventions cannot isolate correspondence as the operative mechanism.

The robustness comparisons are insufficiently specified and potentially circular. It is unclear exactly how the reported VGGT fundamental matrices are obtained in Sections 5.1–5.2—through the synthetic-data-trained probe or from VGGT's predicted cameras. If the former, a benchmark-specific supervised probe is being compared against zero-shot SIFT/SuperGlue pipelines; if the latter, the derivation and failure criteria must be documented. This ambiguity prevents interpretation or reproduction of the main comparative results.

Evidence is narrow and statistically weak: attention and intervention conclusions rely on only five synthetic scenes, with no confidence intervals, variability across assets, random seeds, or significance tests. The synthetic scenes are simple and texture-poor, which predictably disadvantages local-feature baselines, and there is no evaluation on real multi-view datasets or substantially different scene distributions.

The claim that nonzero attention matches on occluded patches demonstrate inpainting, hallucination, or learned data priors is not established. Attention is not itself a correspondence prediction; contextual or positional cues can preserve the same argmax. The study lacks chance baselines, occlusion controls using alternative colors/noise, tests of whether the inferred hidden correspondence is correct in ambiguous cases, and comparison to models with different training priors.

The baseline suite is weak despite the paper citing stronger contemporary matchers: it largely uses SIFT and SuperGlue, omitting LightGlue, LoFTR, MASt3R, and other modern geometry systems. Median error over successful cases plus a thresholded failure rate also obscures the full error distribution and makes comparisons sensitive to the arbitrary 10-pixel threshold.

Several presentation and reproducibility issues compound the scientific concerns: correspondence accuracy is mostly shown as a dense heat map rather than summarized numerically; dataset counts are inconsistent between the main text and supplement; the text alternates among 8-point, 8-point plus RANSAC, and other pipeline descriptions; Figure 6 is described as both medium and large viewpoint change; and implementation details, code/data release information, visibility handling, probe splits, normalization, and intervention mechanics are incomplete. There is also a minor dimensional error in Eq. 1, where a 3D point is declared in R3 but multiplied by a homogeneous 3x4 camera matrix. Overall, the idea has merit, but consequential confounds prevent the manuscript from supporting its main mechanistic and robustness claims.

strengths: The paper asks a timely and important interpretability question: whether a feed-forward 3D foundation model internalizes multi-view geometry or mainly exploits appearance priors. The combination of representation probing, attention analysis, causal interventions, and controlled perturbations is more informative than attention visualization alone.

The layer-wise results form a coherent narrative: cross-view correspondence patterns arise in middle layers, fundamental-matrix decoding improves shortly afterward, and interventions targeting those layers substantially degrade epipolar consistency. The supplementary localized interventions strengthen this evidence.

The controlled ShapeNet/Blender setup provides exact cameras, correspondences, and fundamental matrices while enabling systematic manipulation of viewpoint, focal length, lighting, symmetry, repetition, and occlusion.

The experiments identify both beneficial priors and a potentially undesirable behavior: VGGT is substantially more robust than the tested matching pipelines, yet can infer correspondences in occluded regions. The paper appropriately acknowledges that it has not established implementation of a classical geometric algorithm.

Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best viewed as a Concept & Feasibility/empirical interpretability contribution rather than a new algorithm. Under that framing, its mechanistic insights and experimental methodology are meaningful contributions to computer vision.
weaknesses: The strongest claim—that VGGT has learned epipolar geometry—is not fully isolated by the probing experiment. VGGT is directly supervised for camera intrinsics and extrinsics, from which the fundamental matrix is deterministically computable, and the probe uses the camera token consumed by the camera head. Decodability therefore may reflect supervised camera information rather than an independently emergent geometric mechanism. Baselines probing pixels, DINO features, predicted camera parameters, shuffled representations, and randomly initialized networks would clarify the result.

The two-layer 512-dimensional MLP is a relatively expressive probe and is trained using ground-truth correspondences. Linear-probe results, probe-capacity controls, comparisons against direct camera-to-F computation, and held-out camera-distribution tests are needed. The manuscript also does not clearly specify fundamental-matrix normalization or safeguards against near-zero predictions under the homogeneous Sampson objective.

The correspondence analysis is based on only five synthetic scenes, with no uncertainty estimates, chance levels, or real-image validation. Several broader robustness conclusions use similarly small or incompletely reported samples. This substantially limits confidence that the identified heads and layer transition generalize beyond the chosen objects and renderer.

The interventions provide evidence that selected middle-layer attention entries are functionally important, but the causal interpretation remains partly confounded. Zeroing entire heads or cross-view attention removes more than correspondence information, while the localized experiment lacks equally localized controls targeting non-corresponding patches, random heads in the same layers, or matched amounts of attention mass.

The robustness comparison is not fully representative or controlled. Synthetic, often textureless ShapeNet renders disadvantage SIFT and potentially SuperGlue; stronger and more contemporary alternatives such as LightGlue, LoFTR, MASt3R, or full SfM pipelines are absent. Reporting median error only on successful cases alongside a thresholded failure rate also complicates comparisons; aggregate distributions and confidence intervals would be preferable.

Retained attention maxima at the ground-truth location after masking do not by themselves establish that VGGT hallucinates or inpaints missing correspondences. Contextualized tokens, positional biases, neighboring visible evidence, or coincidental maxima could produce this observation. A stronger test should compare against blank-region controls and evaluate the accuracy and uncertainty of reconstructed occluded 3D content.

The paper is generally clear and candid about limitations, but reproducibility is incomplete: code/data-release information, exact scene counts for every experiment, random seeds, variance across probe training runs, intervention-selection protocol, and full baseline configurations are not provided. These concerns keep the evidence just short of a clear accept despite the promising central insight.

strengths: This is a timely and potentially valuable interpretability study of three influential feed-forward 3D reconstruction models—DUSt3R, VGGT, and Depth Anything 3—rather than an analysis restricted to a single architecture.

The paper combines complementary methods: layer-wise probing, attention-based correspondence measurements, targeted interventions, and controlled input perturbations. Testing on DTU, ETH3D, MipNeRF360, and a controllable ShapeNet dataset gives the descriptive findings useful breadth.

The consistent correspondence patterns across architectures, datasets, view directions, and DA3 model sizes are interesting. In particular, the alignment between mid-layer correspondence activity and improved fundamental-matrix decoding in VGGT/DA3 is a plausible and useful empirical observation.

The controlled synthetic data enable interventions that would be difficult with real imagery, while the supplementary linear-probe, one-epoch, multi-view, feature-similarity, and real-data analyses improve the paper's evidential coverage.

The discussion appropriately acknowledges that attention heads may encode mechanisms besides correspondence and that hallucinated correspondences can be harmful. The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.

Although no contribution type is declared, this work is better assessed as Concept & Feasibility/empirical analysis than as a new algorithm. Under that framing, its main value is the mechanistic evidence and experimental methodology, not benchmark improvement.
weaknesses: The central geometric-understanding claim is overstated. Camera tokens are directly supervised for pose and intrinsics, from which the fundamental matrix is deterministically computable; DUSt3R features are likewise trained for geometry. Decoding F therefore does not establish geometric reasoning “beyond” the training targets. Comparisons with output-derived F, untrained or randomly initialized networks, frozen image features, and suitably capacity-matched controls are needed.

The probing evaluation lacks decisive baselines and uncertainty estimates. A two-layer MLP with hidden width 512 is not a particularly small probe, probes are trained separately on each dataset, and several reported median errors remain large. The paper does not show how these errors compare with trivial predictors, direct camera-output computation, or standard geometric estimators on the same pairs.

The rank analysis is insufficient to establish that probe outputs are valid fundamental matrices. A small sigma_3/sigma_1 also permits rank-1 or nearly zero degeneracies; sigma_2 and matrix normalization should be examined. Moreover, training only with Sampson loss without a rank-2 constraint raises possible degeneracy and numerical-stability concerns that are not addressed.

The intervention experiments do not isolate correspondence as the causal variable. Heads are selected using ground-truth matching performance, but the controls use different early/late layers rather than an equal number of random or low-matching heads from the same layers. Zeroing broad heads, image maps, or 5x5 blocks removes substantial unrelated computation, so the large degradation only demonstrates that these components are important. The most correspondence-specific patch intervention is small for DA3, yet the conclusions remain strong.

DUSt3R intervention results are especially difficult to interpret: 72% of cases become invalid for two intervention types, but results are reported only on valid cases. This selection can substantially bias effect estimates and should instead be incorporated into a common failure-aware metric.

The learned-prior conclusions are not cleanly identified. Nonzero attention to an occluded location may arise from neighboring context, positional structure, global camera constraints, or masking artifacts—not necessarily hallucination or appearance priors. Ablations involving retraining, pretrained-backbone controls, texture randomization, or prior-conflicting scenes would be needed to separate learned priors from geometric inference.

The robustness comparison is narrow and potentially unfavorable to the baselines: a heavily trained end-to-end foundation model is compared mainly with SIFT and SuperGlue plus an eight-point/RANSAC pipeline. Strong contemporary alternatives such as LightGlue, LoFTR, MASt3R, and appropriately tuned reconstruction pipelines are omitted. Key conclusions also rely on a small synthetic test set (five scenes/categories for some analyses), without confidence intervals or statistical tests.

Because the paper's most distinctive claims—causal correspondence formation and separation of geometry from learned priors—are not adequately established by the current controls, the evidence supports an interesting correlational analysis but not yet the stated mechanistic conclusions.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/a0c102686eb741e2b492b39927681399/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a timely and important interpretability question for feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. Studying DUSt3R, VGGT, and DA3 makes the observations more valuable than a single-model case study.

The combination of representation probing, attention analysis, targeted interventions, and controlled input perturbations is thoughtful. Linear-probe, one-epoch, triplet, model-size, and real-dataset analyses provide useful supporting evidence.
The controlled ShapeNet dataset permits systematic variation of viewpoint, focal length, symmetry, repetition, lighting, and occlusion while providing exact geometry and correspondences.

The paper is generally clear and candidly acknowledges that its interventions do not conclusively establish correspondence matching as the sole cause of the observed geometric information. The ambiguous-scene failures are also reported rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Although undeclared, the work is better assessed as Concept & Feasibility/empirical interpretability rather than Algorithms/General: it does not propose a reconstruction algorithm, and its value rests on the validity of its mechanistic evidence. Under that framing, the central evidence is not yet sufficiently controlled.

Decodability of the fundamental matrix does not establish learned geometric reasoning. VGGT and DA3 camera tokens feed heads explicitly supervised for camera intrinsics and pose, from which the fundamental matrix is deterministically computable. The paper's argument that F is not directly supervised therefore does not remove the main confound. Controls based on predicted pose/intrinsics, frozen or randomly initialized networks, input features, and shuffled labels are missing.

The claim that F is “reliably recovered” is inconsistent with the paper's own stated 1–2 pixel guideline. Several reported probe errors are substantially larger, including roughly 30–45 pixels on MipNeRF360. There is no comparison against trivial predictors, the models' final camera outputs, or classical F estimates, so the absolute meaning of the curves is unclear.

The intervention study does not isolate correspondence-specific computation. Heads and layer groups are selected using the same matching statistic, different conditions remove different numbers of heads, and the controls are merely early or late layers rather than layer-, magnitude-, and head-count-matched non-correspondence heads. Zeroing whole heads or large attention regions causes generic network damage and, for DUSt3R, invalid predictions in 72% of cases. Even the paper notes that its results are not conclusive, making the repeated “causal relationship” claim too strong.

The exact intervention operator is insufficiently specified. Statements such as setting keys, attention maps, or activations to zero are not interchangeable around the softmax and residual pathway. Without activation-norm controls or restoration/patching experiments, downstream degradation cannot be attributed specifically to removal of geometric correspondences.

Attention argmax accuracy is treated as evidence of matching without chance, spatial-distance, positional-bias, or appearance-feature baselines. Visibility and occlusion handling are also unclear. Consequently, the apparent alignment between correspondence scores and probe curves may reflect generic cross-view feature matching rather than an epipolar reasoning mechanism.

The learned-prior conclusions are based almost entirely on VGGT and simple synthetic scenes. Attention to a masked ground-truth location may arise from positional bias or mask-based inpainting rather than hallucinated correspondence. The baseline comparison is also weak for 2026: SIFT and SuperGlue omit stronger learned matchers and reconstruction systems such as LightGlue, LoFTR, MASt3R, or modern SfM variants.

Experimental reporting lacks uncertainty, statistical tests, seeds, complete sample counts, probe-capacity controls, and a clear preregistered head-selection procedure. Dense figures report medians without dispersion, while several heatmaps are too small to inspect comfortably. These omissions limit reproducibility and make it difficult to judge whether the claimed layer-wise “phase transition” is robust.

The distinction from the closely related contemporary analysis of multi-view transformers by Stary et al. is not developed sufficiently. Overall, the study contains promising observations, but major confounds undermine its headline mechanistic and causal claims, so the balance favors rejection.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is best viewed as a Concept & Feasibility/empirical interpretability contribution rather than a new-algorithm paper. Under that framing, it addresses an important and timely question: whether feed-forward 3D reconstruction models internalize geometric mechanisms or mainly exploit learned priors.

The study triangulates its central hypothesis using complementary evidence: layer-wise fundamental-matrix probes, attention-based correspondence measurements, feature-similarity analysis, and causal interventions. Applying this framework to VGGT, DA3, and DUSt3R reveals both shared behavior and architecture-specific differences.

The empirical scope is strong. Results span controlled ShapeNet renderings and DTU, ETH3D, MipNeRF360, and SPair71k, with additional analyses of multi-view inputs, linear versus nonlinear probes, DA3 model scales, rank structure, lighting, symmetry, repetition, focal length, and occlusion.

The attention-knockout experiments are particularly valuable: correspondence-selective middle-layer interventions strongly affect VGGT and DA3, while early/late-layer interventions generally have little effect. The paper also appropriately acknowledges that these heads may encode functions beyond correspondence.

The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and generally careful about limitations. In particular, it identifies hallucinated correspondences as a potential downside of learned priors rather than presenting robustness uncritically.
weaknesses: Decodability of the fundamental matrix is weaker evidence for geometric reasoning than the paper sometimes implies. Camera pose and intrinsics are directly supervised in VGGT, and the fundamental matrix is a deterministic function of these quantities. Missing controls include probes on untrained networks, input/backbone features, shuffled labels, dataset-mean predictors, and matrices computed from the models' explicit camera outputs. These would establish whether intermediate-layer probing reveals more than the gradual formation of supervised output variables.

The claimed 'geometric phase transition' and reliable recovery are somewhat overstated. Final root-Sampson errors are often several pixels and reach roughly 30–45 pixels on MipNeRF360, despite the paper itself describing 1–2 pixels as typical for accurate geometry. Reporting normalized-resolution errors and meaningful upper/lower baselines would make these values interpretable. Moreover, a small sigma3/sigma1 ratio alone does not establish a non-degenerate rank-2 matrix; sigma2/sigma1 should also be reported.

The causal controls are incomplete. High-matching heads are compared mainly with random early or late layers, confounding correspondence selectivity with layer location and general layer importance. Same-layer random-head controls, matched attention-mass interventions, random spatial-block controls, and activation patching would better isolate correspondence. Broad zeroing can create distribution shift, while the most localized DA3 effects are quite small. DUSt3R additionally has a 72% invalid-output rate for two intervention types, and reporting only valid cases introduces selection bias.

Head selection and evaluation appear to use the same small ShapeNet test set of five categories/scenes, raising the possibility of post-hoc selection. The intervention plots lack uncertainty estimates, repeated-seed analysis, and statistical tests. Selecting heads on a separate validation set and reporting confidence intervals would materially strengthen the mechanistic conclusions.

The learned-prior conclusions are narrower than the wording suggests. Robustness experiments focus on VGGT and largely on synthetic ShapeNet scenes; nonzero matching to an occluded location does not by itself distinguish semantic inpainting from positional bias, neighboring evidence, or global geometric inference. Occlusion-type controls and validation on natural scenes would be important.

The VGGT comparison against SIFT/SuperGlue pipelines is informative but not fully controlled: an end-to-end foundation model is compared with matching-plus-estimation systems, and the text varies between an eight-point estimator on all matches and RANSAC-based pipelines. Consistent protocols, stronger modern matchers, runtime reporting, and separate accuracy-versus-failure statistics would improve fairness and reproducibility. No clear code or synthetic-data release commitment is provided.
